# Introduction to Computers

## Core ideas and reasoning

A computer accepts data, processes it under stored instructions, produces information and can store results. Data are raw facts; information is data organised into a useful context. The input-process-output-storage cycle explains a task more precisely than saying that a computer thinks. Accuracy depends on correct data and programs: garbage in, garbage out. Computers are fast and consistent but do not independently guarantee truthful conclusions. Classify systems by purpose and scale with context: embedded controllers perform dedicated tasks while general-purpose computers run many applications. Early generations are associated with vacuum tubes, transistors, integrated circuits and microprocessors, though dates and boundaries vary. In a laboratory use stable furniture and a comfortable posture, manage cables, keep liquids away, and shut down safely. A UPS provides temporary backup power to allow saving and orderly shutdown; it is not an indefinite generator. For application questions connect the feature to an actual benefit, such as fast repeated calculations reducing payroll processing time.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

Distinguish data from information using a school example.

Individual test marks are data. A class mean calculated from them is information because it summarises the marks for a purpose.

### Example 2

State two characteristics that make computers useful for payroll.

High speed permits many calculations quickly; consistency allows the same rules to be applied repeatedly. Results still depend on correct data and tax rules.

### Example 3

Why should students save work before a UPS battery is exhausted?

A UPS supplies power only temporarily. Saving and orderly shutdown reduce the risk of losing work when the battery runs out.

### Example 4

Give the importance of standard furniture and an antiglare screen in a computer laboratory.

Suitable standard furniture reduces poor posture, strain and fatigue. An antiglare screen reduces glare and eye strain.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
